title: Twenty distant trans-Neptunian objects outside the Brown & Batygin (2019) sample do not show its perihelion clustering after a survey-bias correction (q > 30 au, a > 230 au)
abstract: Question: The clustering of perihelion longitude (varpi) and orbital poles of the 14 Kuiper-belt objects with q > 30 au and a > 230 au in Brown & Batygin (2019, BB19) is the main evidence for Planet Nine. Do objects that are not in that sample show the same clustering after a correction for survey bias? Method: We used JPL Small-Body Database orbits and Minor Planet Center discovery dates (both 2026-11-12) and wrote an open version of the BB19 bias method: the discovery positions and magnitudes of 5,681 reported objects at r > 30 au trace the survey effort, and each distant orbit is rotated to get its detection probability for each orientation. We compared observed mean canonical vectors with 100,000 bias-weighted draws of uniform orbit angles, and fitted a von Mises varpi model to the BB19 objects to predict the new objects. Results: Our code reproduces the BB19 mean vectors and their varpi clustering (P = 0.022; 0.055 with the BB19 data choices; BB19: 0.04). The 20 other objects with q > 30 au, a > 230 au and a well-determined orbit (U <= 5) have a mean varpi direction of -9 deg, 82 deg from the BB19 direction, and are consistent with uniform orbits (P = 0.48; 0.19 to 0.50 over six effort-map variants; one-sided along the BB19 direction P = 0.27). The BB19-trained model predicts them 3.7 times worse than uniform orbits (log10 BF = -0.57). The test had 78 % power, and the trained model gives a result this unclustered with probability 0.09. A node-only pole test finds no clustering of the new objects toward the BB19 node direction. A BB19-type pole test depends strongly on the assumed inclination distribution and is not reliable. Exploratory: 25 objects at 150 < a <= 230 au cluster near 53 deg (P = 0.04), but many of them are not independent of earlier studies. Limitations: discoveries are only a proxy for survey effort; the pole result depends on latitude weighting; 21 Rubin-era short-arc objects are excluded; 20 objects give moderate power.
